analysis.one_liner: Expands voter access, requires disclosure of big political money, overhauls lobbying and ethics rules, and sets up a Supreme Court code of conduct.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 234-193 with every voting Democrat and no Republicans in favor, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill makes registering and voting easier through automatic and same-day registration, early voting, mail voting, and paper ballots; makes Election Day a federal holiday; and requires independent commissions to draw congressional districts. On money in politics, it expands disclosure of who funds political ads and dark-money groups, cracks down on foreign money, overhauls lobbying and foreign-agent rules, and creates a voluntary small-donor public financing system. It also adds ethics rules for the President, Congress, and the Supreme Court, including 10 years of tax returns for presidential candidates.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters gain the most: automatic registration through government agencies, online registration and updates, same-day and early voting, postage-free mail ballots, paper ballots, disability access, and restoration of voting rights for people completing sentences. Small-dollar donors gain because qualified candidates can get federal matching funds for contributions of $200 or less. Voters in gerrymandered districts gain from independent redistricting commissions. Campaigns for state election officials and foreign-agent enforcement gain teeth, and federal judges get a mandatory ethics code.

how_it_helps.text: Expands voter access through automatic registration via government agencies, online registration and updates, same-day registration, early voting, voting by mail, and postage-free ballots.
Limits removal of voters from the rolls, bans deceptive practices and voter caging, requires paper ballots, and restores federal voting rights to citizens after criminal sentences.

Requires disclosure of who funds political ads including online ads, expands the ban on foreign money in elections, and lifts restrictions blocking the IRS, SEC, and contracting agencies from requiring disclosure of political spending.
Creates a voluntary system where qualified candidates receive federal matching funds for small contributions, plus a voucher pilot program for congressional elections.

Requires a code of conduct for federal judges, restricts the revolving door between government and lobbying, expands Foreign Agents Registration enforcement, and requires presidential and vice presidential candidates to submit 10 years of tax returns.
Requires congressional redistricting be done by independent state commissions instead of legislators who can draw maps favoring themselves.

analysis.who_pays: Wealthy donors, super PACs, and dark-money nonprofit groups lose the ability to spend undisclosed money on elections. Lobbying firms face expanded registration and disclosure requirements. Campaign consultancies and ad firms tied to big-money spending lose some of that business. Taxpayers fund the new election grants, redistricting payments, and the small-donor matching program. States bear new mandates and compliance costs for registration, voting systems, and redistricting.

drawbacks.text: The small-donor matching system, vouchers, and election security grants are taxpayer-funded, and the bill imposes detailed federal mandates on how states run elections, which states' officials argue intrudes on state control of election administration.
Disclosure rules reach into organizations' political spending, including nonprofits, which critics argued burdens donors' and groups' speech and privacy.

The bill bundles many unrelated provisions into one package, so an up-or-down vote forced members to accept everything from redistricting rules to a federal election holiday to executive-branch ethics codes at once.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit to ordinary people is large: easier registration and voting, restored rights, transparent political spending, and harder-to-gerrymander districts. The costs are real but modest by comparison: public money for election infrastructure and matching small donations, plus a genuine shift of election administration toward federal standards that some states view as overreach. The bill is broad and imperfect, but its main transfer runs from concentrated political money toward ordinary voters.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it on March 8, 2019, the Senate read it and placed it on the calendar, and no one ever brought it to a Senate vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced on January 3, 2019 as the House majority's first bill, it was referred to ten committees; the House Administration Committee reported it 6-3, and the other nine committees were discharged.
After three days of floor debate and dozens of amendments, the House passed it 234-193: all 235 voting Democrats in favor, all 193 voting Republicans opposed.
A Republican motion to recommit the bill with instructions on a suffrage title failed 197-228, with six Democrats joining 191 Republicans.

The Senate received it on March 12, 2019, read it twice, and placed it on the Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 39; it never received a Senate vote and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Big donors, dark-money groups, and lobbying firms are better off, because the disclosure rules, foreign-agent enforcement, and small-donor financing that would have narrowed their influence never took effect. The Senate's failure to vote meant the bill's fate was decided without a recorded Senate position.

industries.note: The bill expands who must register as a lobbyist, requires disclosure of lobbyist status at every contact, bans lobbying pay for certain human-rights-violating countries, and creates a dedicated DOJ unit to enforce foreign-agent registration with civil penalties.

industries.industry: Dark-money political nonprofits and super PACs
industries.note: The bill expands disclosure of election spending by organizations, lifts IRS and SEC restrictions on requiring political-spending disclosure, and targets super PAC-candidate coordination, shrinking the pool of undisclosed money.

Online ads would face the same disclosure and disclaimer rules as broadcast ads and platforms would keep public political-ad records; this constrains undisclosed political advertising but is a modest compliance cost relative to the ad market.

Small-donor matching and vouchers would shift some fundraising toward small donors, while election grants fund new voting systems; consultants serving big-dollar clients lose relative business, and voting-machine vendors gain grant-funded purchases.

industries.industry: Voting equipment and election technology vendors
industries.note: Federal grants for compliant paper-ballot systems, risk-limiting audits, and election infrastructure would channel public money toward vendors that supply and upgrade voting systems.
